title: About me
goal: Introduce yourself — name, where you're from, where you live and which languages you speak — and ask others the same.
intro: In this unit you learn the personal pronouns, the two ways of saying 'is' (none at all, or **ଅଛି**) and the negative **ନୁହେଁ** 'is not'. You also meet the main question words, which in Odia simply sit where the answer would go.

vocab.note: Also used by some speakers instead of ମୁଁ ('I') — a regional/stylistic habit.
No gender! With a respectful verb ending (-ନ୍ତି) it means a respected he/she.
Also ମୋର (morô), especially when standing alone: ଏହା ମୋର 'this is mine'.
Before a noun often ତୁମ (tumô): ତୁମ ନାଁ.
Negative of identity: ମୁଁ ଡାକ୍ତର ନୁହେଁ. Forms: ତୁମେ ନୁହଁ, ଆପଣ ନୁହଁନ୍ତି.
ମୁଁ ରହେ, ତୁମେ ରହ, ଆପଣ ରହନ୍ତି (in fast speech often ରୁହନ୍ତି). Command: ରୁହ / ରୁହନ୍ତୁ.
ଆସିଛି 'have come' is used for 'I'm from…'.

phrases.en: Where are you from? (lit. have come from)
I can speak a little Odia.
What is this called in Odia?
Nice to meet you. (lit. meeting you, I felt happy)

grammar.title: Pronouns and 'to be'
grammar.body:
**Identity** ('X is Y') needs no verb in everyday Odia: ମୋ ନାମ ସାମ୍ 'my name [is] Sam', ସେ ଡାକ୍ତର 'he/she [is a] doctor'. (Formal writing adds **ଅଟେ** *ôṭe*.) The negative is **ନୁହେଁ** *nuheṃ* 'is not'.

**Location or state** ('X is in Y', 'X is well') uses **ଅଛି** *ôchhi*, which agrees with the subject:
ମୁଁ ଅଛି *muṃ ôchhi* — I am
ଆମେ ଅଛୁ *ame ôchhu* — we are
ତୁ ଅଛୁ *tu ôchhu* — you are (intimate)
ତୁମେ ଅଛ *tume ôchhô* — you are (familiar)
ଆପଣ ଅଛନ୍ତି *apôṇô ôchhônti* — you are (formal)
ସେ ଅଛି *se ôchhi* — he/she is
ସେ ଅଛନ୍ତି *se ôchhônti* — he/she is (respectful)
ସେମାନେ ଅଛନ୍ତି *semane ôchhônti* — they are

The negative of ଅଛି is **ନାହିଁ** for every person: ସେ ଘରେ ନାହିଁ 'he/she isn't at home'. Notice there is **no gender** anywhere: ସେ is both 'he' and 'she'.

examples.en: He/She (respected) is not at home now.

grammar.title: Question words stay in place
grammar.body:
To ask a question in Odia, put the question word **where the answer would be** — no change of word order and no 'do/does'. Compare: ମୁଁ **ଭୁବନେଶ୍ୱରରେ** ରହେ 'I live in Bhubaneswar' → ଆପଣ **କେଉଁଠି** ରହନ୍ତି? 'Where do you live?'

The main question words: **କ'ଣ** what · **କିଏ** who · **କେଉଁଠି** where · **କେଉଁଠୁ** from where · **କେମିତି** how · **କାହିଁକି** why · **କେବେ** when · **କେତେ** how much/many · **କେଉଁ** which.

Yes/no questions just use rising intonation, optionally with **କି** at the end.

examples.en: Where is your country? / Which country are you from?

dialogue.title: At the tea stall
dialogue.setting: Sam, a British visitor, gets chatting with Bapi at a roadside tea stall in Bhubaneswar.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.native: ନମସ୍କାର। ମୋ ନାମ ସାମ୍। ଆପଣଙ୍କ ନାମ?
lines.roman: nômôskarô. mo namô Sam. apôṇôṅkô namô?
lines.en: Hello. My name is Sam. Your name?

lines.speaker: Bapi
lines.native: ମୋ ନାମ ବାପି। ଆପଣ କେଉଁଠୁ ଆସିଛନ୍ତି?
lines.roman: mo namô Bapi. apôṇô keuṃṭhu asichhônti?
lines.en: My name is Bapi. Where are you from?

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.native: ମୁଁ ଲଣ୍ଡନରୁ ଆସିଛି। ଏବେ ମୁଁ ଭୁବନେଶ୍ୱରରେ ରହେ।
lines.roman: muṃ Lôṇḍônôru asichhi. ebe muṃ Bhubôneswôrôre rôhe.
lines.en: I'm from London. Now I live in Bhubaneswar.

lines.speaker: Bapi
lines.en: Very good! Why are you learning it?

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.native: ମୋ ସାଙ୍ଗମାନେ ଓଡ଼ିଆ। ଆଉ ମୁଁ ଓଡ଼ିଶାକୁ ଭଲ ପାଏ।
lines.roman: mo saṅgômane Oṛia. au muṃ Oṛisaku bhôlô pae.
lines.en: My friends are Odia. And I love Odisha.

culture: Odias will happily switch to English or Hindi with a foreigner — a few sentences of Odia earn real delight. People often ask personal questions early (where you're from, whether you're married, what you do); it is friendly curiosity, not rudeness. Note that many Odias say **ଆମେ** ('we') where English uses 'I', especially in the southern and western districts.
